M8_S01.summary: Dependent origination is the law that whatever arises does so in dependence on conditions: when this is, that comes to be.
body: Paṭicca means 'because of, by reason of'; samuppāda means 'arising, springing up'. Paṭiccasamuppāda is therefore the law of dependent arising, the teaching of conditioned origination.
The Pāḷi definition runs: 'Paccayaṃ paṭicca samuppajjatīti paṭiccasamuppādo' — what arises in dependence on a condition is called dependent origination.
Its basic principle is stated thus: 'Imasmiṃ sati, idaṃ hoti; imasmiṃ asati, idaṃ na hoti' — when this exists, that comes to be; when this does not exist, that does not come to be.

The compendium of conditionality (Paccaya-saṅgaha-vibhāgo) has two parts: the method of dependent arising (Paṭiccasamuppāda-naya) and the method of conditional relations (Paṭṭhāna-naya). The first merely shows one state arising in dependence on another that preceded it; the second analyses the precise way in which one state conditions another.

M8_S02.summary: Twelve links run from ignorance to ageing-and-death, and in this way the whole mass of suffering comes to be.
body: Dependent on ignorance (Avijjā) arise the formations (Saṅkhārā). Dependent on the formations arises rebirth consciousness (Viññāṇa). Dependent on consciousness arise mind and matter (Nāmarūpa).
Dependent on mind and matter arise the six sense bases (Saḷāyatana). Dependent on the six sense bases arises contact (Phassa). Dependent on contact arises feeling (Vedanā).
Dependent on feeling arises craving (Taṇhā). Dependent on craving arises clinging (Upādāna). Dependent on clinging arises becoming (Bhava).

Dependent on becoming there is birth (Jāti). Dependent on birth there arise ageing and death (Jarāmaraṇa), sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief and despair. Thus does this entire mass of suffering come to be.

The twelve links proper are: ignorance, formations, consciousness, mind-and-matter, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and ageing-and-death. Sorrow, lamentation and the rest are by-products (nissandaphala) of birth and are not counted as separate links.

M8_S03.summary: The twelve links span three periods: two belong to the past, eight to the present and two to the future.
body: Ignorance and the formations belong to the past period.
The eight links in the middle — consciousness, mind-and-matter, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging and becoming — belong to the present.
Birth and ageing-and-death belong to the future.
In this way the three periods (tayo addhā) are spread across the chain of twelve links, showing one existence conditioned by the last and conditioning the next.

M8_S04.summary: The twelve links resolve into four groups of five — past causes, present effects, present causes, future effects — making twenty modes joined by three connections.
body: The four groups (catusaṅkhepa) are: (1) five causes belonging to the past, (2) five effects in the present, (3) five causes in the present, and (4) five effects belonging to the future.

Taken together these make twenty modes (vīsatākārā), and the four groups are joined to one another by three connections (tisandhi): between past causes and present effects, between present effects and present causes, and between present causes and future effects.

The source explains how the count is reached: when ignorance and the formations are mentioned, craving, clinging and becoming are implied along with them; conversely, when craving, clinging and becoming are mentioned, ignorance and the formations are implied. Likewise, when birth and ageing-and-death are mentioned, the five effects — consciousness, mind-and-matter, the six sense bases, contact and feeling — are implied.

M8_S05.summary: The twelve links turn as three rounds — defilement, kamma and result — kept going by the two roots, ignorance and craving.
body: The round of defilements (Kilesavaṭṭa) consists of ignorance, craving and clinging.
The round of kamma (Kammavaṭṭa) consists of the formations, and that part of becoming which is called kamma-becoming (kammabhava).
The round of results (Vipākavaṭṭa) consists of that part of becoming called rebirth-becoming (upapattibhava), together with the remaining links.
The two roots (dve mūlāni) are to be understood as ignorance and craving: ignorance stands at the head of the past group, craving at the head of the present one.

As to cessation, the source sums it up: 'By the complete destruction of these causes the round of rebirth comes to an end.' Ignorance itself springs from the taints (āsava) and is fed by the oppression of ageing and death.

M8_S06.summary: Ignorance is the failure to know the Four Noble Truths; in ultimate terms it is the mental factor of delusion, and its opposite is true knowledge.
body: Ignorance is the absence of clarity, the failure to understand, the inability to recognise the truth of things as they are.

The discourses define it thus: not understanding suffering, not understanding its origin, not understanding its cessation, not understanding the way leading to its cessation — this is called ignorance.

The world is impermanent, suffering and not-self, yet it is taken to be permanent, pleasant and a self: that is ignorance. Not understanding the twelve links of dependent origination is likewise ignorance.

In terms of ultimate realities, ignorance is the mental factor of delusion (Moha), from the root 'muh', to be confused, to go astray. Delusion is present in every unwholesome citta and is one of the three unwholesome roots: greed, hatred and delusion.
The opposite of ignorance is true knowledge (Vijjā): clarity, the understanding of the Four Noble Truths, the penetration of dependent origination.

M8_S07.summary: Formations are volition at work in three kinds: demeritorious, meritorious and imperturbable, each producing its own order of results.
body: Formations are what construct, generate and fashion. In terms of ultimate realities, a formation is the mental factor of volition (Cetanā), one of the seven universals.

Demeritorious formations (Apuññābhisaṅkhāra): the volition associated with any of the twelve unwholesome cittas, which drives one to perform the ten unwholesome courses of action through body, speech and mind.

Meritorious formations (Puññābhisaṅkhāra): the volition arising in the 8 sense-sphere wholesome cittas and the 5 form-sphere wholesome cittas; these produce the sense-sphere and form-sphere resultant cittas, and wholesome kamma-born materiality.
Imperturbable formations (Āneñjābhisaṅkhāra): the volition arising in the 4 formless-sphere wholesome cittas, which produces the formless-sphere resultant cittas.
The work of volition is to urge and prompt the other states: it makes the co-arisen factors take hold of the object, completes the task, and marshals those factors to act along with it.
